exposure: Fetal factors (low-birth weight, macrosomia, non-reassuring fetal status, obstetric emergency conditions)
Health service factors (hospital type, quality of intrapartum care, nursing model, nurse work-hours, obstetrician-conducted delivery)
outcome: Birth asphyxia (defined by Apgar scores ≤ 7 at 1 minute)
cohort: The study included 4256 intrapartum chart records from babies in Thailand, categorized by their Apgar scores at one minute of life.
finding: Late-preterm/late-term pregnancies, low birth weight, macrosomia, maternal comorbidity, non-reassuring fetal status, and obstetric emergencies significantly increased the odds of birth asphyxia, while excellent intrapartum care, specific nursing models, low nurse work-hours, and obstetrician-conducted delivery significantly reduced it.
birth_weight: Low-birth weight and macrosomia were included, but specific weight ranges for the entire cohort are not provided.
gest_age: Late-preterm and late-term pregnancies were included, but specific gestational age ranges for the entire cohort are not provided.
